entry.title: LeetCode 274 — H-Index
entry.content:
Problem: H-Index
Difficulty: Medium

🧠 Approach

The key to solving this problem is to understand the definition of h-index.
h-index = The h-index is the largest integer h such that at least h publications each have ≥ h citations.

Knowing this, we just have to sort the numbers in ascending order. Then for each citation, we find the min(citation count, number of papers with >= citation count). Return the max at the end.

⏱️ Complexity

TimeSpace
SolutionO(nlogn)O(n)

✅ Code (Java)

entry.title: LeetCode 679 — 24 Game
entry.content:
Problem: 24 Game
Difficulty: Hard

🧠 Approach

This is quite a challenging problem because I always struggle in visualising the recursion pattern. Although from the tag, we can tell that this is a recursion problem. I didn’t immediately realised how to do this. But here is a picture that illustrates the recursion.

Basically, the idea is that from the original 4 numbers, we select 2 numbers out and perform the 6 possible operations between the 2 numbers. Which 6?

  • a + b
  • a - b
  • b - a
  • a * b
  • a / b
  • b / a

Then, we add the result that we obtain from the said operation back to the array, and again repeat the process mentioned above, choose 2 numbers out, perform the 6 possible operations, until finally, we are left with 1 number, which is also the exit condition of this recursion. Atlas, we check using Math.abs(nums.get(0)-24) < EPS to see whether it is indeed 24. Why do we check whether it is smaller than EPS you ask? Well I asked ChatGPT too haha. Reason is because in certain operations, like 1/3, in Java and Python, this is only stored approximately. When you combine these approximations with other operations, the final result might be 23.9999998 or 24.0000001, not exactly 24.0. This might cause us to wrongly conclude that there is no solution that can result in 24, hence we compare with 1e−6.

⏱️ Complexity

TimeSpace
SolutionT(n) ≤ 6 · n(n-1) · T(n-1)O(n)

✅ Code (Java)

entry.title: LeetCode 837 — New 21 Game
entry.content:
Problem: New 21 Game
Difficulty: Medium

🧠 Approach

Although this problem is labelled as Medium difficulty, I think it should be classified as Hard. I had a really difficult time trying to understand the concept and admittedly used ChatGPT to visualise the pattern. A few things that are intuitive:

  • The probability from k to n(inclusive) is 1.0. Why? Because once you reach k or accidentally overshot k but still below or equal to n, the game terminates, hence the probability of that being n (which is what the question wants) is 1.0.
  • The probability of n+1 to maxPts is 0.0. Rather, this part is not relevant to the probability that we are looking for (which is the probability of the final score being smaller than n).
  • We need to compute dp[x] for all x < k.
    The recurrence is: dp[x] = (dp[x+1] + dp[x+2] + … + dp[x+maxPts]) / maxPts
  • Lastly, we return the value of dp[0]

⏱️ Complexity

TimeSpace
SolutionO(n+MaxPts)O(n+MaxPts)

✅ Code (Java)

entry.title: LeetCode 118 — Pascal's Triangle
entry.content:
Problem: Pascal’s Triangle
Difficulty: Easy

🧠 Approach

The objective of this problem is fairly straightforward, construct a Pascal Triangle of the given number of rows. However, looking at the hints, we know this would involve dynamic programming. The key is then to figure out the repetitve parts since dynamic programming is all about finding the repeating part. We notice that for each row, the first and last element are always 1. The elements in between, are the sum of element in the previous row and previous column and the element in the previous row and the same column. Hence, this is the repeating part.

To solve it, we can:

  1. For each row, create a new ArrayList
  2. If the position is 0 or the last element, we populate it with 1
  3. If the position is not 0 or the last element, we populate it with pascalTriangle.get(row-1).get(col-1) + pascalTriangle.get(row-1).get(col)

⏱️ Complexity

TimeSpace
SolutionO(n2)O(n2)

✅ Code (Java)

entry.title: LeetCode 2348 — Number of Zero-Filled Subarrays
entry.content:
Problem: Number of Zero-Filled Subarrays
Difficulty: Medium

🧠 Approach

This problem is quite clear, it wants us to return the number of ways we can form subarrays of 0, contiguous subarrays. The key is to understand the pattern.
Say we have [0,0,0],

  • the number of ways to form subarray of [0] is 3,
  • the number of ways to form subarray of [0,0] is 2
  • the number of ways to form subarray of [0,0,0] is 1

Hence, from this, we can see that as we are iterating through [0,0,0], we can add 1 + 2 + 3, then reset when we find the next 0 and do the same. Finally, we return the sum of the number of ways.

⏱️ Complexity

TimeSpace
SolutionO(n)O(1)

✅ Code (Java)

entry.title: LeetCode 326 — Power of Three
entry.content:
Problem: Power of Three
Difficulty: Easy

🧠 Approach

To determine if a number is a power of 3, we just need to use recursion to recursively divide n by 3. If it ever gets below 0 or if the modulo of n is ever not 0, then we can return false, else wait till 3/3 == 1, then we return true.

⏱️ Complexity

TimeSpace
SolutionO(log3 n)O(log3 n)

✅ Code (Java)

entry.title: LeetCode 342 — Power of Four
entry.content:
Problem: Power of Four
Difficulty: Easy

🧠 Approach

To determine whether a number is power of 4, we simply need to obtain the power (x) such that when 4 is raised to the power of which, is a whole number. To do this, the most intuitive way would be to obtain the number x and verify if x is a whole number.

Since we have broken down the requirements into 2 mini requirements:

  • Find the power x, such that when 4 is raised to the power of x, equals to n
  • Verify if x is indeed a whole number

we can work on those two requirements individually.

  1. Use Math.log(n) / Math.log(4) to find x
  2. After obtaining the value of x from (1), use the value % 1 == 0 to verify if the number is a whole number

⏱️ Complexity

TimeSpace
SolutionO(1)O(1)

✅ Code (Java)

// Power of Four — Math.log approachclass Solution {    public boolean isPowerOfFour(int n) {        return (Math.log(n) / Math.log(4)) % 1 == 0;     }}

entry.title: LeetCode 1780 — Check if Number is a Sum of Powers of Three
entry.content:
Problem: Check if Number is a Sum of Powers of Three
Difficulty: Medium

🧠 Approach

To determine whether a number is a sum of the powers of three, we can first convert it to base 3. In base 3 format, we can check if it only contains 0 and 1. If it does, then it is a number that is a sum of the powers of 3, else it is not. The reason behind this is because, for each unique power, 0 ~ +ve infinity, the occurrence of 3^unique power is 1 or 0, it is either part of the sum or not part of the sum, it cannot ever be a case where 18(base 10) = 200 (base 3) = 3^2 + 3^2, which makes it no longer distinct (which is what the question requires).

In steps, we simply have to:

  1. Get the base 3 string of the number that is passed in
  2. Check if the base 3 string only contains strictly 1 and 0s

⏱️ Complexity

TimeSpace
SolutionO(log(n))O(log(n))

✅ Code (Java)

entry.title: Jiaksimi.ai — From Fridge to Feast
entry.content:
“Jiak simi?” (what to eat?) — I built Jiaksimi.ai to answer that in seconds.
Pick the ingredients you already have and get 5 great YouTube recipes. Not cooking? I also show 5 nearby restaurants using your location. Try it out here

🍳 What it does

  • Ingredient picker → generates 5 relevant YouTube recipe videos
  • Location-aware suggestions → 5 restaurants nearby with links to open in Google Maps
  • One-click copy/share of a chosen recipe or place
  • Mobile-first UI for quick decisions at the grocery, in the kitchen, or out and about

🛠️ How it works

  1. Ingredient selection
    Users choose ingredients (e.g., chicken, garlic, rice). Jiaksimi builds a search phrase and fetches a small, diverse set of recipe videos from YouTube, then surfaces the top 5.

  2. Video suggestions
    Results are ranked for clarity and relevance (title/description match, recency, channel quality), and de-duplicated so you don’t get five versions of the same dish.

  3. Restaurants nearby
    With the browser’s Geolocation API, the app requests your location and uses Google Maps / Places to find close restaurants. It shows 5 spots with rating, distance, and a deep link to open right in Google Maps.

  4. Fast & simple UX
    Everything happens on one page: swap ingredients, refresh videos, or tap the Eat Out tab to see places around you.

📸 Demo

🧰 Tech Stack

  • Frontend: Vue.js
  • APIs: YouTube search (for recipes), Google Maps / Places (for nearby restaurants)
  • Other: Browser Geolocation, plain CSS/utility classes

Repo: https://github.com/radioblodo/jiaksimi.git

✨ What I learned

  • Designing a decision-making UI that reduces choice overload
  • Handling geolocation permissions and fallbacks when users deny location
  • Normalizing video search results and avoiding duplicates
  • Small performance wins with result caching and cheap re-ranking

📌 Next steps

  • Dietary filters (vegetarian/halal/spicy)
  • “Use up soon” suggestions based on expiring ingredients
  • Open-now + price filters for restaurants
  • Save favorites & recent ingredient sets

entry.title: SafeLink Scanner – A Flutter App to Detect Malicious URLs
entry.content:

entry.title: Building the MDP Android Remote: Lessons in Embedded Systems, Bluetooth, and Team Collaboration
entry.content:
As part of NTU’s Multidisciplinary Design Project (MDP) — a capstone module for final-year Computer Science students — my team developed a mobile-controlled robot capable of both autonomous and manual navigation.

Core components

  • 📱 Android App (my main role)
  • 🍓 Raspberry Pi (Bluetooth receiver + logic relay)
  • 🧠 Pathfinding Algorithm
  • 🔩 STM32 Microcontroller (motor control + sensors)

Although I owned the Android app, I also contributed to Raspberry Pi development, STM32 signal testing, and cross-team integration.

🎯 Project Goals

Built in Kotlin with Jetpack Compose, the app aimed to:

  • Establish a reliable Bluetooth connection to the Raspberry Pi
  • Provide manual robot control with directional buttons
  • Display live feedback from the robot (status, position)
  • Log the robot’s path for testing and visualization

⚙️ Key Technical Highlights

  • Clean, responsive UI with Jetpack Compose
  • Bluetooth socket communication with efficient I/O stream handling
  • Smooth two-way messaging for manual overrides, status polling, and sensor relay
  • Live logs and status tracking for debugging and verification

🧠 What I Learned

  • Calling and parsing JSON between Android and hardware endpoints
  • Working with hardware protocols (Raspberry Pi & STM32 over Bluetooth/serial)
  • Debugging across platforms (Android logs, RPi console, STM32 UART)
  • The value of cross-functional collaboration in embedded + mobile systems

🎥 Project Demo

Watch the demo on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=neUKwJw2OCs

🔗 GitHub Repository
